subject: sync cleanup ownership guard — which files the distributor may delete
context:
house-rules is a kit that distributes agent governance rules from one source repo into ~15 target repos and their git worktrees. `scripts/sync-rules.sh` is the distributor: it copies `cursor/rules/*.mdc` into each target's `.cursor/rules/`, generates a stripped `.md` projection into `.claude/rules/`, and then runs a cleanup pass over those directories.

What changed and why: the cleanup pass used to delete any rule file it did not recognize. That silently destroyed project-authored rules — files a project wrote itself and reasonably put in `.cursor/rules/`. Two real losses were confirmed in the field (`aurion.mdc`, `skills-contributing.md`), recoverable only because they happened to be committed. This change inverts the default. The pass now classifies each unrecognized file three ways: a kit rule being delivered (overwritten, backed up first), a kit rule not being delivered (removed, backed up first), or anything else (kept, and reported to the operator as unmanaged). "Kit rule not being delivered" means a stem on `profiles/retired-rules.list` (a rule the kit renamed or dropped) or — under `--version` — a rule newer than the pinned tag.

A Tier 1 multi-lens pass then found that the first version of this fix introduced three regressions of its own, all now fixed: `--dry-run` never reached the cleanup pass at all, so the documented safety valve previewed only the writes; `--local` (which writes the kit's own fully generated `claude/rules/`) applied the keep-unknown-files policy to a directory where every file is a build artifact, so a renamed rule would stay committed and ship to new adopters with CI green; and a `--version` downgrade stopped removing rules newer than the tag, making pins partial.

Safe mode (default, waived by `--unsafe`) writes a timestamped `.bak` before every destructive operation. `--check` performs no writes and its exit code is a CI contract.
trusted_layers: Do not re-review: the content of the rules themselves; `strip_frontmatter` and the `.mdc`→`.md` projection transform; target discovery and validation (`~/.house-rules-sync-targets` parsing, `validate_target`); the `--version` git-checkout mechanism that populates the pinned source directory; the beads task tracker. Review the ownership/classification logic, the destructive paths, their backup and error handling, the flag interactions, and whether the tests and docs are honest about what the code does.
focus:
The single invariant: a file is removed from a rules directory if and only if the kit owns it. The two failure directions are wildly asymmetric in cost — a false delete is unrecoverable loss of someone's work and is the exact bug this bead exists to fix; a false keep is a retired rule haunting a target. Hunt the false-delete direction hardest, but report both.

Concrete things worth attacking. (1) `in_stem_set` decides ownership by substring-matching a space-delimited string. What file name, list entry, or repo state makes that match when it should not, or miss when it should hit? Note that both stem sets are built by appending onto an initially-empty string, so they carry a leading space. (2) `KIT_KNOWN_STEMS` is read from the kit's *working tree*, deliberately, so a `--version` downgrade still recognizes post-tag rules as kit artifacts. Consider a project that authored `foo.mdc` before the kit ever shipped a rule by that name, and the kit later adds one: under a pin, is that project's file now classified as a kit artifact and deleted? Is that acceptable, and does the `.bak` make it acceptable? (3) `$LOCAL_ONLY` is used as the proxy for "this destination is a generated directory with no project-authored content". Is that proxy exact — is there any invocation where `--local` writes somewhere a human owns, or where a generated directory is written *without* `--local`? (4) `--dry-run` now calls the cleanup pass so it can preview deletions. Verify no write escapes on that path, in either format, including the `mkdir -p`. (5) `backup_file` resolves same-second name collisions with an `[ -e ]` test followed by `cp`. Assess the race and whether the loop can fail to terminate. (6) Error propagation: `retire_or_keep` now returns non-zero when a deletion cannot be made recoverable. Trace every caller — `cleanup_stale`, `sync_cursor_to`, `sync_claude_to`, the main loop, the worktree loop, the `--local` branch — and find any that still discards it. The script runs `set -uo pipefail` without `-e`, so nothing propagates implicitly. (7) The tests: three of the new guards were mutation-verified by reverting the corresponding fix and confirming the matching assertion goes red. Find the ones that were not, and specifically any assertion that would pass against the pre-fix code. (8) `docs/operations.md` and the header comment in the script state the behavioral contract; the previous version of both stated the exact inverse of what the code did. Check them against the code as written.
rules: A file is deleted from a target's rules directory only if the kit owns it. An unrecognized file is kept and reported, never removed.
Every destructive operation — overwrite or delete — writes a recoverable timestamped .bak first when safe mode is on (the default).
A destructive operation that cannot be made recoverable does not happen, and the run exits non-zero so automation can see it.
--dry-run performs no writes and previews every write and every deletion, including the unmanaged-file warnings.
--check performs no writes; its exit code is the contract kit CI depends on.
A generated projection directory (the kit's own claude/rules/, written by --local) contains exactly the projection and nothing else.
--version delivers the rule set the pinned tag describes — no more and no less.
already_addressed: --dry-run did not reach the cleanup pass, making the preview branch unreachable — fixed, cleanup now runs report-only there.
--local applied keep-unknown-files to the kit's generated claude/rules/ — fixed, that path prunes again, and --check --local now fails on an orphan.
--version downgrades stopped removing post-tag rules — fixed via the working-tree union in KIT_KNOWN_STEMS.
A failed deletion backup returned success — fixed in retire_or_keep and at the two call sites (worktree loop, --local) that discarded the return value.
The timestamp/cp/counter idiom had three copies — extracted to backup_file, which also resolves same-second .bak collisions.
A retired-rules.list without a trailing newline silently dropped its last entry — fixed with the `|| [ -n "$stem" ]` read guard.
The rm was unchecked and printed success unconditionally — now checked.
safe_backup_count's summary line described overwrites only while counting deletions too — reworded.
Unmanaged files had no aggregate reporting across a multi-target run — summary line added.
The script header comment and docs/operations.md stated the inverse of the new behavior — both rewritten.
The maintainer obligation to append a renamed rule's stem to retired-rules.list was undeclared — now stated in AGENTS.md.

Test harness defects: setup ran in a command substitution so the cleanup trap never saw the temp dirs (two leaked per run); one negative assertion named the pre-fix wording and could never fail; survival was asserted as name-exists, which a truncating bug would pass; exit codes were not captured; backups were asserted by glob without checking content or stamp shape. All fixed; 12 cases to 28, adding dry-run, --unsafe, --version-downgrade, --local-orphan, and unbackupable-deletion scenarios.
--unsafe writes no backup on the deletion path — accepted as designed, since the overwrite path also skips backups under --unsafe; now explicitly tested rather than implicit.
No CI gate forces a renamed rule's stem onto retired-rules.list — accepted as a real gap, deferred to bead process-kit-ce2.
scripts/init.sh writes to the same directories with no backup at all — accepted as the same defect class on a colder path, deferred to bead process-kit-jjj.
Collapsing retired-rules.list into an inline array at its current single entry — considered and rejected; the file is the surface the deferred CI gate will assert against.
exploit_focus: Demonstrate a concrete counterexample to the ownership invariant: a sequence of file names, retired-rules.list contents, command-line flags, and repository states under which `scripts/sync-rules.sh` deletes a file the kit does not own, or performs a destructive operation that leaves no recoverable copy while the run still reports success and exits 0. Give exact inputs and the line-level code path. Treat every claim in the Context and Already-addressed sections as an assertion to verify rather than a fact — disproving one is itself a finding. If a property holds, prove it per-property against the code rather than reporting that it looks fine. Properties worth targeting in order of severity: (a) a project-authored file is removed; (b) a destructive operation reports success without a recoverable copy existing; (c) `--dry-run` or `--check` performs a write; (d) a retired kit rule survives indefinitely across every target; (e) `--check --local` exits 0 while the generated projection directory is wrong.
